title: Where in the tree do wallet keys live?
dek: BIP 32 derives a tree of keys from one seed. BIP 44 specifies the wallet’s paths. BIPs 84 and 86 specify paths and output types for SegWit and Taproot.

blocks.text: BIP 32 derives a master key and a tree of child keys from a seed. Two wallets can restore the same seed but search different parts of that tree. Each may then miss the other’s coins. They need a shared path convention. BIP 84’s author identifies this compatibility between wallets as the aim.

BIP 44, assigned in 2014, is that agreement. It is an application-layer convention on top of BIP 32 and BIP 43, not a change to the derivation itself. BIP 84 (2017) and BIP 86 (2021) reuse its structure for SegWit and Taproot. All three are recorded as deployed.

figure.title: Five levels below the master key
figure.caption: BIP 44’s first example path. Three hardened levels pick a convention, a coin and an account; below the account line, two public levels number the addresses.

sections.heading: Five levels, each with a job

blocks.text: BIP 44 fixes five levels below the master key: purpose, coin type, account, change and address index. An apostrophe after a number marks hardened derivation, and the first three levels are hardened. The author’s aim was a hierarchy that handles many coins, many accounts, separate receiving and change chains, and millions of addresses per chain.

The purpose is a constant, 44′, which tells software that everything below follows this specification. The coin type gives each coin its own subtree, avoiding address reuse across coins: 0′ for Bitcoin and 1′ for Bitcoin testnet, with a longer list kept outside the BIP in SLIP-0044.

Accounts separate keys into independent identities, numbered from 0. A wallet following BIP 44 does not mix coins between accounts. The BIP compares them to bank accounts for donations, savings or shared expenses.

The change level uses 0 for the external chain and 1 for the internal chain. External addresses are intended for use outside the wallet, such as receiving payments. Internal addresses receive transaction change. Each chain numbers its addresses from 0.

Account discovery starts with account 0 and searches its external chain for transactions. If it finds transactions, it continues with the next account. It stops at the first account with no transaction history. This works because software should not create a new account while the previous one has no history.
BIP 44 gave the gap limit as 20: scanning a chain stops after 20 consecutive unused addresses. Wallet software should warn before a user gives out an address beyond that limit.

BIP 44 scans only external chains, reasoning that internal chains receive only coins that come from the associated external chains. This identifies which accounts have been used. Recovering their funds also requires finding their internal/change outputs.

blocks.title: Finding the accounts again
blocks.caption: How a restored wallet finds its accounts, as BIP 44 describes it. Which addresses are used is made up for the drawing; the gap limit is BIP 44’s.

blocks.summary: Two paths from BIP 44’s example table

blocks.text: BIP 44’s own examples make the pattern concrete. Its table lists 16 paths: the first and second address on the external and change chains, for the first and second account, on Bitcoin and on testnet. The first Bitcoin receiving address of the first account is m/44′/0′/0′/0/0; its first change address is m/44′/0′/0′/1/0.

Follow the same mnemonic down a BIP 84 or BIP 86 path below. Both proposals publish the root, account and address values. The explorer lets you see where the paths share a structure and where their keys differ.

blocks.title: One level at a time
blocks.caption: Published paths from BIPs 84, 86 and 44, stepped from the master key down to the address. A black tab marks a hardened level.

blocks.text: The line between the third and fourth levels matters most. Above it, each step is hardened and needs the parent’s private key. Below it, change and index use public derivation, which anyone holding the parent’s extended public key can do.

An account’s extended public key can derive every receiving and change address in that account. The model demonstrates this with the published account public keys: it re-derives every published address below them. Sharing an account xpub therefore reveals the account’s address history and future addresses. The xpub alone does not let its holder spend funds.

blocks.title: What one account xpub reaches
blocks.caption: BIP 84’s account extended public key and every address its test vectors publish below it, receiving and change, each re-derived from the xpub alone.

blocks.text: For BIP 84’s first receiving address, derivation produces a compressed public key. Its hash supplies the 20 bytes in the output, which the address encodes with Bech32. In BIP 86, the derived key’s x coordinate identifies the internal key. A tweak produces the output key encoded in the address.
The spending witnesses differ too. BIP 84 expects a signature and public key. BIP 86 expects a signature alone. Both leave the scriptSig empty.

blocks.title: What a spend carries
blocks.caption: Both outputs are spent with an empty scriptSig. BIP 84’s witness carries a signature and the public key; BIP 86’s carries only a signature.

blocks.label: Caveat
blocks.text: An account extended public key is not a single address. It exposes every receiving and change address of that account, which is why sharing it is a privacy decision.

BIP 84 and BIP 86 each publish test vectors from the same well-known mnemonic: the root keys, the first account’s keys, and three addresses, two receiving and one change. Step down their paths in Fig. A12.3 above. Every value is derived by this site’s tested BIP 32 code; the account keys and every published leaf value are checked against the vectors when the site is built, and the intermediate values are implied by them.
BIP 44 stops at the key. It defines the path and nothing about the script that key should be used in, nor the address format. Later BIPs treat the purpose value as what signals the script type.

BIP 84 specifies the output type for SegWit version 0. It keeps BIP 44’s path structure and changes only the purpose, 84′. Each key produces a pay-to-witness-public-key-hash output: 0x0014 followed by the key’s 20-byte hash. The address encodes this with Bech32. BIP 84 also assigns different version bytes to extended keys, so they print as zpub and zprv instead of xpub and xprv.

The author’s reason was compatibility in one direction: dedicated SegWit accounts mean only wallets that implement the scheme will find them. BIP 84 is deliberately not backwards compatible, and a wallet that does not know it will not discover the accounts at all.

blocks.title: One seed, three different destinations
blocks.caption: Changing the hardened purpose changes every key below it. BIP 84 and BIP 86 also specify how to turn their keys into output scripts; BIP 44 itself does not.

blocks.text: BIP 86 specifies the output type for Taproot. Purpose 86′ marks keys used as the internal key of a single-key P2TR output. The wallet derives a tweak by hashing the internal key without a script-tree root, then applies it to obtain the output key. This commits to an unspendable script path, as BIP 341 recommends.
The wallet puts the result into a version 1 output: 0x5120 followed by the 32-byte output key. BIP 86 defines no alternate version bytes. Its test vectors print as xprv and xpub.

These conventions help a wallet recover funds from a seed backup. The wallet still needs to search the correct paths and output types. Each convention uses BIP 32 derivation and specifies where to find the keys. BIPs 84 and 86 also specify which outputs to build from them.
